packs.name: Bread box rescue
packs.tactic: Tear day-old bread into cubes, toss with oil and salt, and toast at 375F until crisp for croutons, or layer the same cubes with ripe tomatoes and a quick vinaigrette for a ten-minute panzanella. Trimmed crusts and ends can dry on the counter overnight and become breadcrumbs in a spice grinder. If the loaf will not be used within a few days, slice and freeze it straight from the bag - frozen slices toast like fresh.

packs.name: Wilted spinach revival
packs.tactic: Wilted spinach is still salad-worthy after ten minutes in ice water; if it is too far gone, flash it in a hot pan with garlic until just collapsed, or blitz it into a soup, dal, or a pesto made with whatever hard cheese is around. For leafy herbs and greens you will not reach in time, blend with a little oil and freeze flat in a bag for instant flavor cubes.

packs.name: Floppy carrots
packs.tactic: Re-crisp limp carrots for twenty minutes in a bowl of ice water, then use them raw; if they stay bendy, roast them cut side down at 425F until the edges brown, or grate them into a pilaf, fritter batter, or a vinegar-dressed carrot salad. Soft carrots that still smell sweet cook exactly like crisp ones once heat and salt are involved.

packs.name: Bananas past their prime
packs.tactic: Spotted, soft bananas are the sweetest ones: mash two into pancake or muffin batter, stir one into oatmeal as it cooks, or blend with yogurt and freeze in a shallow tub for a one-ingredient soft-serve. Peel the rest, break into chunks, and freeze in a bag - frozen chunks disappear into smoothies and banana bread later.

packs.name: Yesterday's rice
packs.tactic: Cold cooked rice is the best fried rice: break up the clumps, fry hard with aromatics and whatever vegetables need using, and season with soy sauce at the end - or simmer it into a gingery rice porridge for breakfast. Handle leftovers exactly as the food-safety rulebook specifies; see safetyRuleRefs on this pack before cooking.
packs.notes: Cooked-rice handling and reheating are governed by data/food-safety/rules.json; this pack links those rules instead of restating them.

packs.name: Too-soft tomatoes
packs.tactic: Overripe tomatoes want heat, not crispness: halve them, cook down with a splash of oil and a smashed garlic clove for fifteen minutes, and you have a quick sauce, or roast them cut side up at 400F and pile onto toast. A squeeze of vinegar at the end wakes up flavor that refrigeration muted.

packs.name: Mealy apples
packs.tactic: Mealiness disappears under heat: dice and simmer mealy apples with a spoonful of water and cinnamon into a chunky applesauce, bake them into a crisp or quick bread, or fry slices in butter until caramelized and serve with pancakes. Peel first if the skin has toughened, and keep the peels for tea.

packs.name: Limp celery
packs.tactic: Stand celery stalks in a jar of cold water in the fridge for a few hours to restore their snap, or slice them straight into the pot: limp celery still melts perfectly into a mirepoix, a bean soup, or a braise. Leaves and ends are stock gold - collect them in a freezer bag until soup day.

packs.name: Bendy zucchini
packs.tactic: Grate soft zucchini, salt it in a colander for ten minutes, squeeze dry, and bind with an egg and a handful of flour for fritters - or fold the grated squash into muffin batter or a simmering soup where its texture vanishes. If the skin is wrinkled, peel strips off and cook the flesh; it will season the dish more than it shows.

packs.name: Broccoli going yellow
packs.tactic: Yellow-tinged broccoli tastes stronger but cooks the same once trimmed: cut into florets, roast at high heat until the tips char, or simmer soft and blitz into a cheddar or garlic soup. Use it soon and cook it thoroughly; for anything past this point, defer to the food-safety rulebook on when to discard produce.
